extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and litigators preparing or defending AIA proceedings (IPR) before the PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on filing and litigating AIA proceedings (especially IPR): petition drafting limits and content, strategic timing, preliminary replies, discovery (depositions), motions to compel, expert declarations, and motions to strike evidence before the PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition content and filing limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions must include detailed identification of grounds, claim constructions, and where each claim element is found in the prior art; filings are subject to a 14,000-word limit per petition (37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b); 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)(1)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to incorporate arguments by reference (37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(3)). If over the 14,000-word limit, petitioner may seek waiver under 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)(2). The petition should stand on its own with detailed identification of grounds and claim constructions, including construction of means-plus-function terms and mapping of elements to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple/parallel petitions discouraged
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board and the Consolidated Trial Practice Guide advise that 'one petition should be sufficient' and that multiple petitions 'may place a substantial and unnecessary burden on the Board and the patent owner' and 'are not necessary in the vast majority of cases.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing multiple petitions to circumvent word limits or to split issues is generally disfavored; consider whether multiple petitions are truly necessary before filing more than one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scope of petitions relative to district-court contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice: wait for the patent owner's preliminary infringement contentions from district court to see which claims are asserted before deciding which claims and issues to challenge in an IPR petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a district court infringement matter is pending, obtaining the plaintiff's preliminary infringement contentions can inform which claims are actually in dispute and allow a more targeted PTAB petition, avoiding unnecessary challenges and conserving word count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and proper use of Preliminary Replies to a POPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner may seek leave to file a Preliminary Reply to respond to Patent Owner Preliminary Response (POPR), but such a request must show good cause (37 C.F.R. § 42.108(c)); replies may only respond to the patent owner preliminary response and sur-replies only to replies (37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking a Preliminary Reply, focus on issues not foreseeable at the time of filing the petition. Potential proper bases include Fintiv/314(a) considerations, 325(d), whether a reference qualifies as prior art, changes in law or PTAB guidance, or interim claim constructions/rulings in district court. Consider limiting the reply (e.g., 5 pages) to unforeseen issues rather than re-arguing the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv/314(a) discretionary denial considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may deny institution under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) (Fintiv) when institution would interfere with a parallel district court proceeding—e.g., when the PTAB trial is scheduled shortly before a district court final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a petition is filed while parallel district-court litigation is ongoing, analyze Fintiv factors and consider whether scheduling or other circumstances make institution unlikely; raise appropriate arguments in a Preliminary Reply if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and weight of expert declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert declarations that largely 'parrot' the petition or simply restate petition arguments without additional evidence or reasoning may be entitled to little weight (see Xerox Corp. v. Bytemark, Inc.) but are not automatically disregarded; the Board evaluates the specific testimony to determine weight (Equipmentshare.com Inc. v. Ahern Rentals, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on an expert declaration solely to restate petition arguments. Declarations should provide independent reasoning, analysis, or evidence supporting the petition's positions; otherwise the Board may give such testimony little or no weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to make declarants available for cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine discovery includes cross-examination of affidavit testimony prepared for the proceeding (37 C.F.R. § 42.51); a party presenting a witness's testimony by affidavit should arrange to make the witness available for cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you present declaration evidence, arrange for deposition/cross-examination of the declarant. Failure to make a declarant available (including non-party witnesses) can be a basis for motions to strike or other relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to compel testimony — authorization and foreign testimony requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A party seeking to compel testimony or production must file a motion for authorization; the motion must describe the general relevance and identify the witness (37 C.F.R. § 42.52). For testimony sought outside the United States, the motion must identify the foreign country, explain why the witness can be compelled there (procedures), and demonstrate reasonable efforts to secure the witness's agreement to testify in the U.S. (37 C.F.R. § 42.52(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking testimony from witnesses abroad, be prepared to: (a) identify the foreign country, (b) describe compulsion procedures and estimated timing, and (c) show you tried and failed to obtain voluntary U.S. testimony (including offering to pay travel expenses). Motions to compel generally require prior Board authorization (37 C.F.R. § 42.20(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and practice for motions to strike declaration evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where cross-examination is unavailable despite best efforts, the Board may exercise its authority to strike such a declaration under 37 C.F.R. § 42.12(a),(b). The Trial Practice Guide states a party presenting affidavit testimony should arrange for cross-examination; otherwise the Board may strike it (citing John’s Lone Star Distrib., Inc. v. Thermolife Int’l, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot depose an opposing declarant and have made reasonable efforts to secure deposition, consider a motion to strike. The Board may strike declarations where there is an inability to cross-examine coupled with insufficient justification for the witness's unavailability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting tactics that may be improper or ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics like creative citation shortcuts to save space (e.g., compressing citations or offloading explanations into an expert declaration) may run afoul of rules that prohibit incorporation by reference and require detailed identification in the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trying to game word limits through citation tricks or by hiding substantive argument in declarations. Ensure the petition contains the necessary detailed grounds and constructions so it complies with 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.6, 42.104 and the Board’s expectations.
